nodes.description: The trigger, and it is deliberately named for the gene rather than for one lesion, because two mechanistically different allele classes sit under it. Roughly half of reported variants truncate the aggrecan core protein - frameshifts, nonsense alleles and splice-site changes - including the single-base-pair insertion in the exon 12 variable repeat region that founded the series in the SEDK kindred. The remainder are missense substitutions, and these are not scattered: those linked to osteochondritis dissecans cluster in the C-type lectin repeat of the C-terminal G3 domain. The two classes are carried to separate downstream nodes below because what they do to the protein is not the same thing.

nodes.description: What the C-type lectin missense alleles actually do, and the part of the story that took three studies and changed twice. The G3 C-type lectin repeat is how aggrecan engages the surrounding network - tenascins and fibulins - and the p.V2303M substitution abolishes those interactions in binding assays. The original report also found the variant protein present in patient cartilage by mass spectrometry, which read as an argument against a secretion defect. Later work on three further G3 missense families measured secretion directly and found it reduced, for recombinant protein and for full-length aggrecan from patient cartilage alike. Both results stand: the protein is present, and less of it gets out.

nodes.description: The step that explains the entry's most counter-intuitive feature. Short stature usually comes with a delayed bone age; here it comes with an advanced one. In aggrecan-deficient chick growth plates the hedgehog, FGF and BMP signalling that paces the plate is abnormal and chondrocytes hypertrophy early, and because hypertrophy is what triggers vascular invasion and ossification, the plate both matures and closes ahead of schedule. Clinically the advanced bone age is therefore a readout of reduced remaining growth potential rather than a separate lesion - which is why these children stop growing at a median of 12 years despite normally timed puberty, and why predicting their adult height from bone age fails.
